title: Plan, organise and support project meetings and workshops

lessons.title: Planning a project meeting or workshop
lessons.html:
Why planning matters

Projects in agricultural extension often depend on meetings and workshops: a steering committee for an irrigation scheme, a planning workshop with a vegetable co-operative, or a training workshop on record keeping for small livestock farmers. A poorly planned meeting wastes people's time and money. Farmers may travel far by taxi or bakkie and lose a day's work to attend, so every meeting must be worth it.

Start with the purpose

Agree with the project leader what the meeting must achieve. Is it to share information, make decisions, solve a problem, plan activities or train people? The purpose decides who must attend, how long it takes and what format works best.

Planning checklist

  1. Purpose and expected outcomes: written in one or two sentences.
  2. Participants: who must attend, who should be informed, and who has the authority to make decisions.
  3. Date and time: avoid planting, harvest, pension pay-out days and community events such as funerals. Check with key people first.
  4. Venue: a community hall, school, farmer support centre or shaded area on the farm. Check size, toilets, water, electricity and access for people with disabilities.
  5. Budget: venue hire, catering, transport, printing, interpretation and equipment, all in rand and approved before spending.
  6. Agenda: topics, presenters and time for each item.
  7. Resources: projector, flipcharts, markers, attendance register, name tags and handouts.

The agenda

A good agenda lists the meeting title, date, time, venue, purpose and each item with a time and a responsible person. Put the most important decisions early, when people are fresh. Include breaks for longer workshops. Send the agenda and any reading documents to participants at least a few days in advance so they come prepared.

lessons.title: Organising logistics and inviting participants
lessons.html:
Getting the logistics right

Once the plan is approved, you organise the details. Use a logistics checklist and tick items off as they are done.

Invitations

  • Send invitations early, usually two weeks before for a workshop and one week before for a regular meeting.
  • Use the channels people actually use: WhatsApp, SMS, phone calls, letters, or announcements through the dip tank committee, ward councillor or traditional council.
  • Include the purpose, date, start and end time, venue with directions, what to bring and whom to contact.
  • Ask people to confirm attendance by a set date so that you can plan catering and seating.
  • Send a reminder one or two days before.

Venue and equipment

Confirm the venue booking in writing. Visit or phone the day before to check that it is clean and open. Arrange seating to suit the purpose: rows for presentations, a circle or small tables for discussion. Test the projector, extension cords and sound system. During loadshedding, plan for a generator, a charged laptop or a flipchart-only session.

Catering and transport

Order catering based on confirmed numbers plus a small margin. Provide water, especially in summer. If transport is part of the budget, confirm pick-up points and times with the driver and the participants.

Materials

Print the agenda, attendance register, handouts and evaluation forms. Prepare documents in the languages participants understand. Arrange an interpreter if needed.

Safety and comfort

Know where the exits and first aid kit are. For outdoor workshops, plan for shade, sun and rain. Keep emergency contact numbers on hand.

Keep all quotes, orders and invoices for the project file, and follow your organisation's procurement rules.

lessons.title: Supporting the meeting and following up
lessons.html:
On the day

Arrive early, at least an hour before the start. Set up the room, test equipment, place the attendance register at the door and welcome people as they arrive. Make sure everyone signs the register, since many projects must report attendance to funders.

During the meeting, your support role includes:

  • Helping the chairperson or facilitator keep to time.
  • Handling equipment and handing out materials.
  • Managing late arrivals quietly.
  • Making sure tea and lunch are ready on time.
  • Taking minutes or notes.

Taking minutes

Minutes are the official record of the meeting. They should include the date, venue, people present and apologies, and for each agenda item a short summary of discussion, decisions made and actions agreed. For each action, record what must be done, who will do it and by when. Do not try to write every word. Focus on decisions and actions.

ActionResponsibleDue date
Get three quotes for borehole repairCo-op secretary15 March
Book soil sampling with extension officerChairperson30 March

After the meeting

  1. Pack up, return equipment and leave the venue clean.
  2. Type up the minutes, have them checked by the chairperson and send them to participants within a few days.
  3. Update the project action list and follow up on actions before the next meeting.
  4. Pay suppliers and file invoices.
  5. Review evaluation forms and note what to improve next time.

Key points

  • Start with a clear purpose, then plan participants, date, venue, budget and agenda.
  • Avoid dates that clash with planting, harvest, pay-out days or community events.
  • Send invitations early through channels people use, and send reminders.
  • Record decisions and actions with responsible persons and due dates.
  • Distribute minutes quickly and follow up on actions.
